claims.text: The target material is a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy thin coating on a conventional metal substrate.
An epsilon phase is present and mechanically active in the FeNiCrCoCu coating.
Non-basal pyramidal <c + a> slip is activated in the coating's epsilon phase.
Deformation twinning is activated in the coating's epsilon phase.
A lower-than-ideal c/a ratio promotes non-basal pyramidal <c + a> slip and deformation twinning in epsilon-phase transformative HEAs.
Alloying additions can alter the intrinsic c/a ratio of an h.c.p. epsilon phase.
Processing and deformation can change the c/a ratio of epsilon martensite in transformative HEAs.
Transformation volume change affects epsilon-phase lattice parameters through dependence on microstructure and stress state.
Activation of epsilon-phase pyramidal slip and twinning governs the coating's overall wear resistance during high-temperature sliding.
Activation of epsilon-phase pyramidal slip and twinning governs microscopic deformation during high-temperature sliding.
Changing alloying elements and processing conditions to alter c/a ratio and transformation volume change will improve wear resistance.
The controlled change will reduce microscopic deformation.
The predicted behavior applies in a high-temperature sliding regime.
The comparison baseline is a conventional metal substrate without a high-entropy-alloy coating.
Failure of the coated specimen to show significant improvements in wear rate and microscopic deformation relative to the uncoated substrate would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention proposes changing alloying and processing within a coating, but the stated baseline and falsification comparison use an uncoated substrate. This does not isolate the proposed c/a-ratio or transformation-volume intervention relative to a baseline coating.

The mechanism invokes activation of slip and twinning, which are microscopic deformation modes, while the outcome predicts reduced microscopic deformation without defining a distinct deformation metric or explaining how increased activation produces the reduction.
